title: Why is Hamilton getting so many penalties? - F1 Q&A
description: BBC Sport F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions after the Hungarian Grand Prix.
fullText:
McLaren's Lando Norris won the Hungarian Grand Prix from pole position, his first victory since becoming world champion.

Red Bull's Max Verstappen was second and Mercedes' championship leader Kimi Antonelli completed the podium in third.

Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton was given a five-second penalty for speeding in the pit lane and finished fifth behind his team-mate Charles Leclerc.

F1 will now go on a summer break and return for the Dutch Grand Prix, from 21-23 August.

BBC Sport F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions after the race at the Hungaroring.

Why is Lewis Hamilton getting so many penalties at the moment? With his vast experience, you would have thought that at least some of them could have been avoided - John

Lewis Hamilton has had four penalties in the past three grands prix, which does seem a lot for a seven-time world champion.

But just because events happen in a statistical cluster does not necessarily mean there is any kind of wider pattern behind them.

In this case, it does just seem as if it's one of those things - a series of events that can happen at any time, and just happen to have happened when they did.

The penalties are all very different.

At Silverstone, Hamilton was penalised for moving before the start, after his car jumped forward briefly and then stopped before the lights went out.

At Spa, he was given a five-second penalty for causing a collision with George Russell at Les Combes on the first lap.

And in Hungary, there was a three-place grid drop for impeding Oscar Piastri in qualifying, and a five-second penalty in the race for going 0.1km/h over the pit-lane speed limit while racing Kimi Antonelli out of the pits when both stopped under the late virtual safety car.

Hamilton said on Sunday after the race: "Ultimately, the last three races have been pretty bad from my side.

"Silverstone start - we talked in the drivers' briefing the fact that they're inconsistent with this stuff. Drivers in the past have moved and not been penalised.

"We discussed that, as long as you're not moving when the last lights are on, you shouldn't be penalised. I wasn't out of my [start] box. And they agreed. So they're looking into that for the future.

"The last race, even the driver I collided with said that it was just a racing incident. I think that one was not needed. But that cost me a lot of points.

"And then the one yesterday was really just unfortunate. I take responsibility for ultimately being on track. I should have looked in my mirrors. But I thought everyone would have been at the end of the first lap. The information I got was right at the end. A communication error.

"I'll work hard to try and come back. There's still a lot of positives to take. I'm going to try and make sure I don't give them any reason to penalise me."

Norris and McLaren almost perfect as Ferrari flounder

Complete weekend for Norris but poor result for Sainz - driver ratings

Do you think Aston Martin's upgrade could persuade Fernando Alonso to continue as a driver? - Robert

Fernando Alonso is out of contract at the end of the year and has a decision to make as to whether to stay in F1 next year.

He is 45 on Wednesday and has been doing this for 25 years. He wants to be sure he makes the right decision because, unlike the last time he stepped away from F1 in 2018, there will be no coming back this time when he leaves.

Alonso has been discussing his mindset on his future all season. In a nutshell, he has said he will continue to race, but he does not know whether that will be in F1.

He enjoys the competition of F1, but - like most of his colleagues - he is not enamoured by the new generation of engines and the need for energy management and how that has detracted from the driving experience.

He has been less clear about how the competitiveness of the Aston Martin-Honda package will affect his decision.

Alonso is a difficult person to read, and he can be gnomic when he speaks.

My feeling is he is leaning towards continuing, but only if he feels he can be confident Aston Martin will be in decent shape next year. Another year like the first half of this one - stuck at the back, racing no-one - has no appeal at all.

In Hungary, the debut of the new Aston Martin car was a significantly positive step. Alonso made it out of first qualifying for the first time this year, and the race pace was strong.

The team, it turns out, had hoped for an improvement of about two seconds a lap from the aerodynamic improvements and weight-saving, and, at least in Hungary, that was pretty much delivered. That's a remarkable step - pretty much unheard of in terms of mid-season upgrades.

It was also important because the upgrade was a proving test for the factory's ability to deliver developments that worked - which had not been the case for three years.

The next step is the new Honda engine, which will make its race debut at the Dutch Grand Prix after the summer break.

The Honda is a long way behind the other power units - something in the region of of about 1.5secs per lap off the best, Aston Martin believe internally.

The impending upgrade will not narrow that gap completely. But it is hoped that it will narrow about a third of it.

This is equally important for Alonso. He will want to see proof that Honda can deliver improvement - not least because he has prior experience from his time at McLaren from 2015-17 of Honda's promises not living up to reality.

I'm told he will wait to see how that goes before properly considering his decision on his future.

The team want him to stay. Team principal Adrian Newey said at the weekend: "Fernando is an amazing driver. He brings huge amounts to the team, both in his feedback and his ability.

"So, for us, of course it's important. I'm pretty confident that Fernando is enjoying his time with us and that we will continue with our relationship."

After positive progress in previous seasons, how much longer can Williams go on without making some drastic changes as they slip down the order this year? And how much longer can they retain Carlos Sainz? - Craig

This year has been a shock for Williams.

They had spent the past two seasons talking about how everything had been focused on developing the team so it could make a big step towards the front under the new 2026 rules, and instead they have taken a big step backwards.

Team principal James Vowles did not expect it, but has said that it happened because the rules ended up stress-testing the factory and exposing weakness they did not previously know existed.

Asked why the factory was not ready, given he had been there since 2023, he says, effectively, you only know what you don't know when you discover it.

Vowles concludes: "Never let a good crisis go to waste. The amount of changes we have made have put us into a very good situation in the future, and I don't think we would have made them if we'd partially succeeded this winter. So, as painful as it's been, I believe we had to go through it."

Cynics might say they have heard that sort of thing from Vowles before - when the car was late in 2024, for example.

As for the drivers, there is no question that Carlos Sainz and Alex Albon are frustrated, but the reality is they do not have a lot of options.

The driver market is a bit stuck at the moment while everyone waits to find out what Max Verstappen does.

If he moves, though, it's unlikely that either Williams driver would be Red Bull's first choice to replace him.

Verstappen would be going to either Mercedes or McLaren and the expectation would be that the drivers he is likely to replace - George Russell and Oscar Piastri - would end up swapping.

Beyond that, there are only midfield teams available.

In Sainz's case, he turned down Audi two years ago to go to Williams, and in any case, they seem happy with their current line-up.

Alpine? Is it worth going there instead of Williams?

Racing Bulls is not an option. Haas would be below either's ambitions. Cadillac even more so - and if one of their drivers move on it would likely only be to make way for reserve driver Colton Herta.

In reality, the only viable alternative might be Aston Martin - but there is only a seat there if Fernando Alonso decides to leave F1.

There were numerous blue-flag infringements in the race, which had or would have had a decisive effect on the results. How can these situations be avoided in the future? - Juha

Usually, the drivers are warned about cars coming up to lap them in three ways - a blue-flag indicator on their steering wheel, blue-light panels trackside, and traditional blue flags.

But there was a problem with the link between the F1 timing system and the FIA race-control system in Hungary - it was dropping out and kicking back in.

That meant the system erroneously believed some cars had been lapped because they were not showing up on the correct timing loops, so it started showing blue flags when no-one had been lapped.

When this was realised, the automated blue-flag system was disconnected and the FIA relied on marshals showing blue flags or pressing the buttons that operate the blue-light panels trackside.

The teams were alerted to the problem as soon as it happened, but it did lead to the odd issue.

The most high-profile of these was Carlos Sainz colliding with Oscar Piastri as the McLaren driver came up to lap him.

This potentially cost Piastri the lead, as Lando Norris was about to pit at the time, and came out only marginally ahead of his team-mate.

Sainz received a five-second penalty for that incident, as did Haas driver Oliver Bearman for failing to respect blue flags when he was being lapped by Red Bull's Isack Hadjar.

For the future, the FIA is working on an update that would calculate expected car position in the case of an irregular refresh rate from the F1 timing system.

title: Why Chelsea want to sign older players
description: Chelsea are targeting deals for Maxence Lacroix, Jordan Henderson and Danny Welbeck - three experienced heads, in an age when the focus has been on youth.
fullText:
Chelsea are targeting deals for Maxence Lacroix, Danny Welbeck and Jordan Henderson - and the ages of the experienced trio seem to signal a major change in transfer tactics from the Blues.

At 26, it could be said that Crystal Palace and France defence Lacroix is in his prime, but the £52m target is still notably older than other recent Blues signings.

It has been two years since Chelsea signed a player older than Lacroix, and Tosin Adarabioyo was only marginally older when he arrived three months before turning 27.

Meanwhile, Brighton striker Welbeck is 35 and keen to move to Stamford Bridge, and Brentford and England midfielder Henderson is 36.

Welbeck's potential arrival could mean he replaces 23-year-old Liam Delap in the first-team picture.

That is despite Delap having been considered one of the Premier League's most exciting young strikers when Chelsea signed him from Ipswich Town last year.

So does this signal a deliberate change in recruitment strategy - prioritising experience over youth? And what might Chelsea have learned from recent seasons?

In the months that followed the club's takeover four years ago, then manager Thomas Tuchel went on a spending spree.

His first major signing was Manchester City winger Raheem Sterling - aged 27 at the time - for up to £50m including add-ons. After winning four Premier League titles at City and helping England reach the semi-finals of the 2018 World Cup, there was much excitement.

Sterling at Chelsea didn't work out though. Despite moments of brilliance, Sterling struggled for form and fitness as the team went on to finish 12th in the 2022-23 season.

For a player reportedly earning over £300,000 a week, his performances fell well short of expectations. Sterling eventually left on a free transfer in January 2026.

Kalidou Koulibaly's arrival from Napoli for £33m also didn't end well. Rated at the time as one of European club football's top centre-backs, the Senegalese player - then 31 - was out of the door after just one season, joining Al-Hilal.

Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang is another experienced player whose time at Stamford Bridge was short-lived. The former AC Milan, Borussia Dortmund and Arsenal striker signed from Barcelona for £10.3m on the final day of the summer transfer window - just days before Tuchel's sacking.

Aubameyang - 33 when he joined - struggled to find form or game time under subsequent bosses Graham Potter and Frank Lampard and, like Sterling, ended up leaving the club on a free transfer.

After such a poor return from their investment, it is perhaps no surprise that there was a shift in recruitment policy, as Chelsea switched their focus to signing younger players.

Let's start here with the success stories.

Chelsea made a major investment in a World Cup winner in January 2023 when they signed Argentina star Enzo Fernandez from Benfica for a then-British record fee of £107m. The move came just two weeks after his 22nd birthday.

Across the 2024-25 and 2025-26 seasons, Fernandez registered an impressive 24 assists in all competitions - including the Club World Cup - trailing only Bruno Fernandes and Mohamed Salah among Premier League players.

Chelsea made another nine-figure move just seven months later to sign Moises Caicedo - then 21 - from Brighton.

His £100m price tag - rising to a potential £115m - seemed hard to justify at first as the Ecuadorian had a slow start at Stamford Bridge.

Since then, Caicedo has established himself as one of the Premier League's leading midfielders.

Caicedo was the joint leader for interceptions in the Premier League last season (59, the same number as James Garner of Everton).

The initial £40m the club paid Manchester City for Cole Palmer - also 21 at the time in September 2023 - has also looked like money well spent.

Palmer was the club's top scorer in his first season.

Only Erling Haaland (76), Salah (54) and Ollie Watkins (51) have scored more goals than Palmer, with 47, in the Premier League since he joined.

Then there are the signings that haven't worked out.

Mykhailo Mudryk was 22 when he joined Chelsea from Shakhtar Donetsk for an initial fee of £62m, potentially rising to £89m including add-ons. The Ukraine winger, now 25, has been sidelined for over 18 months after an "adverse finding in a routine urine test" led to a provisional suspension in December 2024.

The winger has since been served with a four-year ban by the Football Association and has lodged an appeal with the Court of Arbitration for Sport.

Joao Felix struggled to make an impact during two stints at Chelsea. His first loan spell in 2023 at the age of 23 started with a red card in his first game.

A permanent move followed a year later but he struggled to justify the fee - somewhere in the region of £45m - and scored just once in 12 Premier League games before being sold to Al-Nassr.

After joining from Leicester for about £70m at the age of 21, Wesley Fofana's time at Chelsea has been plagued by injury.

The France international, who was not selected for his country's World Cup squad, could be under scrutiny as the club look to reduce the size of their squad.

What next for £70m Fofana at Chelsea?

The Chelsea academy stars looking to break through

For a club to have spent as much as Chelsea, it is no surprise fans might be frustrated with the returns - or lack of them.

The 12th-placed Premier League finish in 2022-23 - the first season since the takeover by the BlueCo consortium - was clearly a big disappointment.

Improvements followed, with sixth and fourth in the next two campaigns signalling strides in the right direction, but finishing 10th last season was another big blow.

Since 2022, Chelsea have won two trophies: the Conference League and the Club World Cup.

But for owners with such big ambitions, they will surely feel like their expectations haven't yet been met.

If his previous managerial approach is anything to go by, Xabi Alonso favours a blend of youth and experience.

The Spaniard signed four players over the age of 27 for the 2023-24 season at Bayer Leverkusen. They included Granit Xhaka and Alejandro Grimaldo - two key players in their Bundesliga title-winning side.

Another four players over the age of 27 came the following season.

It could be a similar story now at Chelsea.

Owner Behdad Eghbali said Chelsea would "tweak" their model and add experience to what he still believes is a strong core of young players, including Cole Palmer, Moises Caicedo and Levi Colwill.

Welbeck joining Chelsea would be another sign of a shift in strategy.

Their move for him follows attempts to sign 33-year-old midfielder Granit Xhaka from Sunderland, with the Black Cats refusing to sell the Switzerland captain.

Although the arrival of Rogers, 23, fits the club's preferred policy of signing younger players, he brings significant Premier League experience.

The Blues are also expected to complete a £52m move for Lacroix, 26 - further Premier League-ready experience.

It is clear that Welbeck's arrival would leave Chelsea with an abundance of attacking options for a season when they are not involved in European competition so do not necessarily need such resources.

At his age, Welbeck may be content to provide cover for Joao Pedro, but the move would represent bad news for several other forwards.

Nicolas Jackson is open to leaving, while Delap and Emmanuel Emegha had hoped to establish themselves under Alonso.

Nevertheless, the Chelsea manager is getting what he wants: experience and strong personalities to address shortcomings that contributed to the team's 10th-place finish in the Premier League last season.

title: France braces for fourth major heatwave as crews tackle Bordeaux blaze

fullText:
BORDEAUX, France, July 28 (Reuters) - France was bracing for its fourth major heatwave of the year on ‌Tuesday, as soaring temperatures and tinder-dry conditions across the southwest piled pressure ‌on crews battling a giant wildfire in the Bordeaux region.

Temperatures in Bordeaux are forecast to ​reach 33 degrees Celsius (91 degrees Fahrenheit) during the day, around 7 degrees above the average high between 1961 and 1990, according to the Reuters Climate Monitor.

"The situation we are dealing with today is the most severe we have ever recorded, the ‌toughest since the Second World ⁠War," President Emmanuel Macron, who flew to the area, said on Monday evening.

Fire crews had contained the blaze overnight, but ⁠the situation remained difficult, Nathalie Delattre, Senator for Gironde which covers the city of Bordeaux, said.

"Everything will depend on how the firefighters on the ground get on," ​she told ​BFM TV on Tuesday.

France is going through ​an unprecedented wildfire season. The ‌area burned has already surpassed the previous record year of 2022.

The Landes area, southwest of Bordeaux, is covered by pine forests, which become highly flammable when dry. The fire has burned down 42,000 hectares so far.

Authorities have evacuated about 220,000 people, including holidaymakers and local residents.

In the area of Biscarrosse, a town ‌about 40 km south, which was hit by ​another wildfire last week, the situation has ​improved and some 15,000 evacuated people ​were gradually allowed back home in the town and a ‌campsite nearby, the local administration said ​on X.

"However, (the favourable) ​development does not mean the risk has been eliminated. Flare-ups remain possible, particularly due to weather conditions (wind, drought, etc.)," it said.

Temperatures were set to ​increase in the region ‌from the afternoon and peak at 37 degrees Celsius on Wednesday, ​weather office Meteo France said.

title: Devastating European wildfires in maps - and how they're being tackled
description: A blaze near Bordeaux has torn through more than 162 sq miles (420 sq km) in less than four days, while the Madrid region is seeing its worst fires ever.
fullText:
Wildfires are tearing through France and Spain, forcing more than 300,000 people to evacuate their homes.

France has seen its worst fires in two decades, while officials in the Spanish capital Madrid say they are the worst the region has ever experienced.

It follows a sweltering summer of heatwaves across Europe that have seen temperatures soar above 40C (104F) in many places.

Separate wildfires in the regions outside Madrid have together burned about 297 sq miles (770 sq km), authorities estimate - an area larger than Madrid itself.

In France, the worst affected area is Gironde, around the city of Bordeaux, where more than 200,000 people have been forced from their homes.

The blaze has spread rapidly, tearing through forests and fields in France's famous wine region, and burning more than 162 sq miles (420 sq km) in less than four days - an area roughly four times the size of Paris.

It is now just nine miles (15km) from the south of Bordeaux.

The fires have also threatened a number of sensitive military and industrial sites in the area, including facilities that work on French ballistic missiles, rocket motors, and the processing of hazardous chemicals.

Satellite imagery above Gironde shows vast areas of scorched, blackened earth, with smoke drifting inland to the east.

The fires have become so extreme they have created their own giant fire thunderstorm.

A rare weather event, storms like these are formed when heat from the wildfires makes the air above the fire rise rapidly, carrying smoke, ash and water vapour high into the atmosphere.

As the air rises, it cools, and the water vapour condenses into a cloud. If the fire is powerful enough and the atmosphere is unstable, that cloud can grow into a cumulonimbus - the same type of cloud associated with thunderstorms.

If these clouds then become large enough, they can produce their own lightning, which can then start new fires. They can also occasionally bring hail and rain.

These extreme and unpredictable conditions make the fires all the more difficult to stop.

To combat them, French firefighters have been using planes loaded with fire retardant, as well as planes like the Canadair, which can scoop 6,000 litres of water from lakes or the sea in 12 seconds and drop it directly on the fires.

On dangerous days, loaded aircraft patrol high-risk areas before any fires have been reported, so they can drop within minutes of a sighting. Planes often fly in a continuous shuttle while retardant is laid along the edges of the fire and ground crews attack the flames directly.

In Gironde, about 2,500 firefighters, 1,500 military personnel, and 1,200 police officers and gendarmes have been involved in tackling the blaze.

But even with these numbers, Gironde official Jean Luc Gleyze told the BBC that authorities don't have enough people to combat the fires.

"We don't have enough people and enough trucks and even I think France don't have enough," he said.

Around the town of Lacanau, bulldozers, diggers and mechanical shovels have been used to carve a firebreak that is 100m (328ft) wide at points, according to French media.

A firebreak is essentially a stretch of land that has been stripped of all vegetation to stop the fire from spreading - removing any potential fuel before the fire has a chance to reach it.

Spanish teams have been using many of the same techniques to tackle their wildfires, which are on course to become the worst the country has seen in two decades.

Francisco Martin, a government delegate in Madrid, described the fires as "undoubtedly the largest fire in the history of the Madrid region".

This summer's fires have been aided by the hotter, drier conditions caused by climate change, which allow fires to spread faster and burn more fiercely.

Many on the ground - in both Spain and France - are fearful that the coming week could see worsening conditions, with high pressure forecast to bring dry, settled and increasingly hot temperatures.

President Donald Trump told a crowd in Michigan that the White House has ordered 250 Cadillac Escalades, the flagship sport utility vehicle in the luxury auto brand's lineup, for his presidential motorcade.

"The one and only Escalade," he said toward the beginning of a roughly one-hour-long address. "You know we ordered, I think, 250 Escalades, right? We ordered 250 Escalades…. We look sharp in those Escalades."

The 2026 Escalade has a manufacturer's suggested retail price starting in the low $90,000's, though upgrades take it well north of six figures. Its high-performance V-series runs about $170,000.

"Our guys are very spoiled," he said. "They're very spoiled. They like the Escalade. So do I."

Endorsement of the Escalade, introduced in 1998, by hip-hop artists and in pop culture in the late 1990s and early 2000s helped reshape its image as status symbol and change Cadillac's reputation as a car for older generations, according to a history of the car posted by Al Ghandi Auto. It appeared in a Jay-Z music video and in a freeway chase scene of "The Matrix Reloaded."

Cadillac, the preferred brand of many previous presidential administrations, also produces Trump's presidential limousine, "a custom-built, highly secure fortress on wheels" known as "The Beast," according to the automaker.

In his speech, the president praised the Chevrolet Silverado, GMC Sierra and "the world-famous Hummer" as "some of America's most iconic vehicles."

"Thank you to the auto workers, the technicians, the mechanics, the welders, the engineers at General Motors," he said. "There's no finer group of people. It was workers like you who built this country, and now it's the men and women like you who are making it bigger, better, richer and stronger than ever before."

General Motors, based in Detroit, recently reported stronger-than-expected second-quarter results despite a 31% net drop in income, citing strong American support for the company's pickups and SUVs.

fullText:
In opening statements, state argued Meta’s own research showed it harmed teens while firm’s attorneys pointed to transparency

The long-awaited trial between the social media company Meta and the state of Tennessee began proceedings on Monday. Attorneys for Tennessee told a jury in Nashville that Meta, which owns Instagram and Facebook, disregarded internal research about its platform’s impact on teenagers, while the company sought ⁠to maximize profit from those young users.

During ⁠opening statements in a seven-week ​trial in state court, the state’s lawyers said Meta researchers repeatedly flagged teenagers’ compulsive use of the platform – leading to eating disorders, depression and self-harm. But despite those warnings, Meta did not ⁠disable features such as autoplay, notifications and infinite scroll which, the lawyers said, were designed to keep teens on Instagram as long as possible and increase the number of ads they viewed.

An attorney for Meta countered the company has been transparent ⁠about the risks teens face on Instagram and the amount of dangerous content it finds. The company works hard to find problems and fix them, the attorney said.

Tennessee’s lawsuit is one of 42 cases brought against Meta by individual states across the US. It comes after the company suffered a damaging loss in New Mexico in March, where a jury found the company liable for harming children and ordered it to pay $375m in civil penalties. It also comes as thousands of other lawsuits have been filed against Meta and other social media companies by families, school districts and state attorneys general.

The lawsuit in Tennessee, filed by attorney general Jonathan Skrmetti’s office, seeks financial penalties ‌and a court order directing Instagram to modify aspects of the platform that the state says are harmful to teens’ mental health.

If the jury finds ‌Meta liable, the trial will enter a second phase where the judge will decide damages.

During the opening statements, Tom Cartmell, a lawyer for the state, said Instagram triggers dopamine hits that promote addiction and that has a particularly strong impact on the brains of kids.

Cartmell also showed the jury an internal document from 2017 in which Meta product managers wrote that features such as notifications and infinite scroll “are inherently at odds with well-being” and said that the company needed to warn ​the public.

“This warning never came,” Cartmell said.

Kevin Huff, a lawyer for Meta, said documents such as those Cartmell cited are proof that the company is searching for problems on its platforms, so it can improve them. The company has developed tools to help limit problematic use of Instagram, Huff said, and seeks to empower teachers and parents to help keep teens safe.

“We think the evidence will show that Meta is doing its part and empowering others to ​do their part, because protecting teens online is a ​shared responsibility,” Huff said. “It takes a village.”

The next lawsuit over social media addiction and harm to children is slated to go to trial next month in Oakland, California. It will be the first federal trial against the social media companies, including Meta, YouTube, TikTok and Snap, and was brought by attorneys general from 29 states.

fullText:
Salamanca City Central says it is pausing project with Realbotix as it addresses concerns including data privacy

A New York school district has walked back plans to introduce a humanoid robot at its high school after the proposal sparked backlash from educators and community members.

The Salamanca City Central school district announced on 24 July in a social media post that its pilot project with Toronto-based tech company Realbotix had been put on hold “while we work through enhanced student data privacy agreements with the New York State Education Department and continue engaging with our community and stakeholders”.

“Ensuring that appropriate privacy protections are in place and incorporating input from our community are important parts of the process. We appreciate your patience and will share additional updates as they become available,” added the school district, which is located on the Seneca Nation reservation in upstate New York and serves a large Native American population.

The reversal came after widespread criticism of the program, which would have brought a humanoid robot named Sally to Salamanca high school. According to a Realbotix press release issued in June, the approximately $58,000 robot with silicone skin and brown hair was intended to use “natural conversation, facial expressions and real-time interaction to create engaging, hands-on learning experiences”.

“The robot aims to encourage student participation and provide early exposure to emerging technologies,” the company also said.

A little more than two years before Friday’s announcement, Realbotix acquired Simulacra, a Las Vegas-based company that manufactures sex dolls.

The New York State United Teachers union had condemned the plans calling for high schoolers to be taught by a humanoid robot.

“A robot built by a company associated with sex dolls has no business in our classrooms,” Melinda Person, the union president, said in a 23 July statement.

Person added: “Our students don’t need robots. They need real relationships with caring adults. Educators notice when students are struggling, celebrate when they succeed and help them discover who they can become. No robot can do that, no matter how lifelike its skin or specific its regional accent.”

Lacey Pihlblad, the president of the Salamanca Teachers’ Association and a teacher at the high school, also criticized the proposal, saying: “The Salamanca teachers’ union as a whole is concerned about the background of the company of Realbotix. We’re very concerned about the security of the software that they’re implementing, and whether or not the data will be stored, how it will be gathered, [and] the recording capabilities.”

Other educators also questioned why the pilot program was being launched at a school serving a large Native American population.

Speaking to the Guardian recently, Sierra May Abrams, a substitute teacher at Salamanca high school, said: “Out of all the schools in New York state, let alone in the US, they chose to experiment on Native American children yet again.”

Abrams alluded to the history of brutality at Native American boarding schools in the US and said: “Our culture is struggling to stay alive due to the impact of [that] and what they did to our elders. We live on the only reservation located in a city so it’s just absolutely insane that we’re the ones ‘testing it out’.”

Following the Salamanca district’s decision to pause the program, Realbotix’s CEO, Andrew Kiguel, told New York Focus: “We fully respect any decision the school makes and encourage thorough due diligence by all parties involved.

“We want the program to be demonstrably safe, fully district-approved, and strongly supported by teachers … We stand firmly behind [the program] as a supportive tool designed to assist teachers and students, not replace them.”

fullText:
SEATTLE (AP) — For veteran linebacker Dante Fowler, Jr., the chance to join the Seattle Seahawks wasn't something he was going to pass up again.

After finishing with three sacks and 15 total tackles with Dallas last season, Fowler signed a one-year contract with the Seahawks in May worth up to $5 million.

Fowler, the No. 3 overall draft pick by the Jacksonville Jaguars in 2015, considered signing in Seattle last year before opting to go back to the Cowboys. But after an aggressive sales pitch from Seahawks veteran and former Cowboys teammate DeMarcus Lawrence, along with a visit to the team headquarters, he knew the time was finally right.

“You can see why they won the Super Bowl, whether it's on or off the field,” Fowler said. “It’s actually pretty cool to see the camaraderie here from the top to the bottom, front office and the team. It’s a great group of guys. You come into this building happy, and you come in looking forward to going to work.”

Fowler is stepping into an enviable situation for a free agent signee, with the Seahawks returning the majority of last year’s dominant defense. Linebacker Boye Mafe (Cincinnati), safety Coby Bryant (Chicago), and cornerback Riq Woolen (Philadelphia) were the most notable losses, but the Seahawks are expected to once again be among the league's best.

Even on a defense as heralded as Seattle, a veteran presence like Fowler can still help make everyone better.

“The way he comes in, he works. I think from a football aspect, like what he’s going to bring to that room, pass rush-wise, Lord, like, he’s able to get off the rock,” linebacker Ernest Jones IV said. “He has so many moves in his bag, and it’s only going to make the guys around him better.”

Fowler was also attracted to Seattle by the presence of defensive coordinator Aden Durde, who Fowler first worked with in Atlanta in 2020 when Durde was a defensive assistant, then in Dallas when Durde coached the Cowboys’ defensive line.

Durde tried hard to recruit Fowler to Seattle last season, and Fowler is excited to once again be working with the Seahawks British-born coach.

“Just to see the way he’s grown throughout his career, and being my defensive line coach at the Cowboys to now his role as a defensive coordinator here, is very awesome,” Fowler said.

Along with Durde, Fowler is eager to continue working with Seattle’s strength and conditioning staff, which he says is the best he’s ever worked with.

Fowler credits the staff for getting him into fantastic shape, which gives him optimism that he’ll have a big year like in 2024, when he had 10 1/2 sacks and 39 tackles with Washington.

“I feel like how it felt when I played in Washington with the Commanders,” Fowler said. “I just knew I was going to have a great season just because of the work that I put in all season, and how good of a shape I was. So I feel like that.”

Head coach Mike Macdonald has already started to feel Fowler’s impact three days into training camp.

“You want to affect the quarterback, but not too much at this point," Macdonald said, “so he’s doing great. He’s getting used to how we roll here, and I think he’s enjoying his time, which is positive. Definitely seeing flashes for sure.”

While he wasn’t a member of last year’s Super Bowl-winning squad, Fowler hasn’t struggled to fit in on a Seahawks team that already has plenty of star talent on defense.

“I just fall in line and do what I’m supposed to do,” Fowler said. “They already had a great defense before we got here, and they won a Super Bowl. It was the best defense in the world last year. So my job is to just fall in line and do whatever I’ve got to do to make this defense upgrade a little bit more.”

title: 49ers star gives glowing early scouting report on rookie defender

fullText:
The San Francisco 49ers have their rookies and veterans back in the building, as they officially started training camp on Sunday at their SAP Performance Facility with offensive line coach and assistant head coach Chris Foerester filling in for Kyle Shanahan.

One of the more surprising aspects of the team's first training camp session was defensive end Nick Bosa's involvement after the star pass rusher suffered a torn ACL last year. It was unclear whether or not he'd miss some time to start the 2026 season, but it looks like he should be ready to go for Week 1.

While everyone is excited to have Bosa back, the five-time Pro Bowler shared just how impressed he's been with one of his teammates - rookie defensive end Romello Height.

“For rookie wise, I’ve never seen a guy come in and get the scheme as quickly and seamlessly as he has," Bosa told Brian Murphy and Markus Boucher of KNBR on Monday. "Even when vets come in, who haven’t played in this scheme, he’s gotten it quicker than I did. Just the way he picked it up, it seems like it’s second nature to him and he’s SUPER explosive. He’s got a bag of tricks in his pass-rush that you can tell he’s been coached well. He’s a little older and that might be a part of it for a rookie, but I think he’s going to contribute pretty quickly.”

Height, 25, was San Francisco's first of two picks in the third round of the 2026 NFL draft. He spent six seasons in college between four different schools, as he played two years at Auburn, two years at USC, one at Georgia Tech and one at Texas Tech. He left Monday's practice on a cart, but avoided serious injury. The team told reporters the rookie was dealing with cramps during the second training camp session.

In 48 games over six years, Height recorded 111 tackles, 16.5 sacks, four forced fumbles, two fumble recoveries and one interception.

If Height can prove himself throughout camp and the preseason, he could play a huge role for the 49ers in 2026, especially if 2025 first-round pick Mykel Williams misses time early on while he recovers from his own torn ACL.

title: I Guess I'm Playing the Long Game Now
description: My latest post on the difficulties of young parenthood has loosened something in the back of my …
fullText:
My latest post on the difficulties of young parenthood has loosened something in the back of my mind. In a few others’ too; thank you so much for your encouraging messages! These small replies might not seem like much to you, but they do to me. So again, thank you.

I’d like to take a shot at solving the problems that surfaced. I’m playing The Long Game now—I should enjoy the daily small wins, knowing that it’ll be an exhausting ultramarathon, not a short sprint. I never fully realise this but a friend of mine might be right: I usually overly focus on the negatives instead of cherishing what I already have.

So how to turn that around? Perhaps I should simply repeat an experiment from 2013. In one of the first blog posts ever to appear on this site, I explain how I end my days with happy thoughts. I never thought I’d cross-reference to something more than 10 years old but there it is. The idea is simple: instead of letting frustration roar at full speed inside, try to shift your attention to small wins. Tiny little things that unlocked a smile are enough. A daddy, look! perhaps.

This is what I came up with in my journal:

The “small wins” page spread should cover the entire month and is divided into four columns: (1) day indication, (2) small win description/remarks, (3) mood, and (4) physique. It should be dead-easy to fill in otherwise I won’t be doing it, hence the Studio Ghibli stamps. Totoro happy? Me happy. Totoro OK? Me so-so. Totoro with umbrella? Me expecting emotional rainfall. I have yet to stamp a happy Totoro in there but the point is mostly to what you’d call “get a grip”.

For that reason, I don’t want to write anything neutral or negative in the second column. I’ll be needing a fine nib to squeeze everything in there. Maybe I should ignore the “remarks” title altogether. I wrote “TIRED” next to the first umbrella, but should I?

A considerate reader told me they take more pictures of their kids just running around in and around the house to look back on fondly afterwards. That’s sound advice. We should do that more often and forget about it in the many hectic moments. I re-read three journals from a few years ago today and the pasted in photos (mostly from the pocket printer) always make me smile. Our daughter found the photos of the baby funny: “hey look, that’s mom and little brother!” “No it’s not, it’s you when you were a little baby!” “oh wow! but now I already am high up in the sky!”. Note to self: order new pocket printer sheets.

The Long Game means leaving short bursts of dopamine behind. And yet I find myself buying fountain pens—the last purchase was three years ago—or scrolling through BoardGameGeek’s The Hotness list to see what else I can pick up after I sold a few ones just lying around on the shelf. I often try to escape into my laptop or book or whatever when things get heated with the kids. I notice I grab my smartphone during breakfast while I never did that before. The Long Game means noticing, admitting, and trying to change behaviour. I guess stage one is as good as any place to start.

The youngest gave me a really hard time today. In August I’ll be playing daddy-day-care for both of them and I already feel slight hints of panic rolling my way. The Long Game means acknowledging it’s going to be a mess but we’re going to be okay regardless. As my favourite philosopher Michel de Montaigne said: the purpose of life is to live it.

A short sprint would mean this to be over in no-time. The look back into my previous journals already taught me that The Long Game is more than fast enough: one day you’re writing “hey today the first one said bye bye and walked off onto the street for the first time!” and the next day you find yourself writing “next month the youngest turns one what happened??”

title: Essential Words
description: Differences between “essential vocabulary” lists, 1953 vs. 2023
fullText:
Look through the words scattered around this page. Every one of them is among the most commonly used words in the English language.

They come from a 2023 list of about 2,800 words, shown to cover over 90% of general English use, intended for people learning the language.

This 2023 list is an update of an earlier one, made in 1953, which identified about 2,300 words as the essential vocabulary to everyday life at the time.

Between the two lists, 70 years apart, about 600 words were dropped, and over 1,100 were added. The rest remained as is.

Some of the changes make immediate sense: Telegraph dropped out; computer was added, along with website and blog. Tobacco was replaced by cigarette. Motherhood became mom, and dad was added too, though fatherhood was never on the list to begin with. The world changed and vocabulary surely followed.

But also: apple didn’t make the new list. Neither did fork, soap, umbrella or leaf, for example. It’s not that these things vanished from everyday life, but many hands-on words became less central to the core vocabulary. Dog stayed; goat and donkey didn’t. Bread stayed; breadmaking ingredients—flour and wheat—dropped. Cook is on the new list. Boil, bake, and fry are not.

And many of the words that were added, such as mortgage, corporation, appropriate, analysis, fairly, and despite, don’t look anything like the ones that were discarded. In fact, they are mostly abstract concepts that don’t look like anything at all.

How the Words We Teach English Language Learners Changed, and What That Says About Us

These “essential vocabulary” lists are called the General Service List (1953) and the New General Service List (2013, revised in 2023).

They were designed as teaching tools for people learning English as a second language, built from real-world usage data and extensively tested. The aim was a vocabulary list with as few words and as much coverage of everyday English usage. That coverage is high, over 90% for the 2023 list1 and about 84% for the 1953 list.2 To account for that much of the language, they had to track a significant portion of whatever people were actually reading and saying. A word earned its place by appearing often enough, across enough contexts, to be hard to avoid for the average person in an English-speaking society. Open the word lists panel on the right to browse through all the entries in both lists.

While these were practical tools, built to capture which words people need most, the answer also doubles as a snapshot of ordinary life, 70 years apart: what people were expected to engage with, and had to deal with, in their daily lives.

Treating the lists as an indirect record of day-to-day life, I went through the differences between them from a few angles: what the words were about, how tangible were they, and to which parts of speech they belonged.

I started by using a common linguistics research tool3 that sorted all of the words by meaning. It assigned each word to one of 21 subject categories, based on typical usage: Food and Farming, the Body and the Self, Government and Public, Language and Communication, and so on. Together, they suggested what kind of world each list was built for.

Data 

The categories that shrank are mostly those that have to do with the immediate, physical world, while the gains are those furthest from it.

To better see this, the categories can be oriented spatially. Some categories describe you: your body and emotions. Some describe what’s immediately around you: food, objects, and the natural world. Others name systems you participate in: government, institutions, society, and culture. And some have no location at all: abstract concepts, reasoning, and processes. When we look at the data grouped by physical scope, the pattern of change seems to point in a specific direction.

In hindsight, the shift makes sense. By 1957, four years after the original list was published, white-collar workers outnumbered blue-collar for the first time in US history. And by 2000, fewer than one in four workers did manual labor. The stuff people encountered in their daily lives, what they needed to talk about, and the systems they had to navigate all changed.

The vocabulary lists, built from the language of their respective eras, tracked those changes. The shifts reflect a life that moved further from its own making: less tied to tools, animals, food, and the body; more tied to national or global institutions, categories, systems, and ideas.

The new vocabulary—mortgage, legislation, perspective, involvement, improvement, assumption, evaluation—are words you can’t weigh, point to, or hold in your hand. These words shape your life, but they do it without occupying physical space.

To better understand whether there was a shift in vocabulary describing the physical world, I compared each word to a database that rates its tangibility on a scale of 1 to 5 (called a “concreteness rating4”). A rating of 5 means you can experience the word directly with your senses, while a rating of 1 means you can’t.

Kernel density estimation, bandwidth 0.08 · Data 

This shift matters because abstract and concrete words are processed by our brains in different ways. When you read axe, your brain doesn’t just decode letters, it reaches for something: an image, a weight, or a gesture. The word activates both a verbal label and a sensory trace. Psychologists call this dual coding:5 Concrete words travel through two channels, verbal and sensory; abstract words travel through one. Two channels mean two retrieval pathways, which is why concrete words are “stickier,” easier to hold in a line of thought and faster to recall. Abstract words, on the other hand, are purely verbal, and have to be understood through language alone.

To put it another way: Concrete words are easier for us to process because they are bundled with a web of associations, tactile experiences, and memories that anchor their meaning. Here’s a more detailed view of the shift away from concrete language:

Data 

While concrete words have sensory grounding to carry their meaning, abstract words rely on other parts of speech to specify, soften, or sharpen what they mean. That help tends to come from one particular corner of the language: adverbs.

The 2023 list contains more words overall (2,809 vs. 2,284). All changes mentioned in the text reflect each category's share of its list, not raw counts. Data 

Axe doesn’t need an adverb to modify it; you know what it is. But acceptable, relevant, and adequate come with conditions, qualifications, and degrees that need to be spelled out. Adverbs do precisely that: language to calibrate language. 
Look through all the adverbs that were added:

Most of the adverbs specify degree, frequency, certainty, and extent. Some hedge (somewhat, partly, relatively, possibly, approximately). Others assert (absolutely, definitely, entirely, exactly, precisely). They're all doing the same kind of work: Take a statement and tell you how much of it is true, how often, and how certain. It’s as if the world now requires you to be more precise about everything.

Bread survived both lists. Flour, wheat, harvest and bake didn’t. The word for what sustains us remained essential, while the words for how we’d make it weren’t. That might be the most honest summary of what happened.

The world that made the 2023 list is more regulated, more connected, and in many ways more capable than the one behind the 1953 list. It’s a world further than our kitchen or home, reaching across economies, institutions, and democracies.

Today's vocabulary reflects a life that isn’t self-contained, but rather more systemic. It’s not so much about what’s within arm’s reach, but more about the larger world we navigate through. That sort of long-distance connection requires a particular kind of language: expansive, abstract, and precise. And language, it turns out, can’t help itself. It keeps track.

I compared two prominent vocabulary lists for English learners: the General Service List (GSL, 1953; 2,284 words) and the New General Service List (NGSL 1.2, 2023; 2,809 words). I labeled words appearing on both lists as “remained” (1,656), words only on the 1953 list as “removed” (628), and words only on the 2023 list as “added” (1,153).

The GSL words came from the Simple English Wiktionary GSL. The NGSL words came from the official NGSL 1.2 file (“alphabetized and lemmatized for research”).
The NGSL uses lemmas (one entry per word family); the GSL sometimes lists inflected forms as separate headwords. These lists track word forms deemed worth teaching based on frequency and usefulness, not abstract concepts. For example, the word being is on the GSL as its own headword and was not included in the NGSL, But this doesn’t mean the concept of existence left the language. In the NGSL it falls under be, which is on both lists.

Both lists were built for teaching, but external research suggests each covers a large share of everyday language use. About 84% of general English for the GSL and about 90% for the NGSL, depending on the text and how words are counted. I did not re-run those corpus analyses myself. I take the published materials as given and rely on coverage figures from the list authors and from follow-up studies (including an independent check on American English by Stoeckel, 2019 – see footnotes). That’s why the differences between the lists felt worth examining as more than a curriculum update, with the caveat that neither list is a neutral census of culture.

All tagged words: remained, removed, and added, with semantic tags, concreteness ratings, and part-of-speech labels are in this public spreadsheet. You can also browse the word lists in the word-list panel on the right side of this page.

Each word was tagged with the UCREL Semantic Analysis System (USAS), using the 21 top-level categories. USAS also assigns much finer sub-categories (there are hundreds), but I stayed at the top level so the charts could show broad shifts without splitting the words into overly granular bins.

I chose not to correct mislabels. For example, hammer, nail, and wax are all tagged “General and Abstract Terms”, but in USAS’s finer tags, they read as actions (“to hammer,” “to nail,” “to wax”), not objects. Out of context, many of these words go multiple ways, and it didn’t feel right to override that case by case; USAS is an established linguistic framework, and swapping in my own judgment would mix two different standards.

For the second chart, I grouped USAS’s 21 categories into five “scope” domains (self, local, institutional, social, abstract). That grouping is my editorial choice, not part of USAS. It came from noticing a spatial quality to the trends seen across the 21 categories.

Concreteness ratings come from Brysbaert et al. (2014). I used these as-is. Six words weren’t in the database and were left out of the concreteness charts: as, dialog, english, gaiety, madden, and old-fashioned.

Parts of speech were tagged with NLTK, simplified to five categories. Here I did intervene, but only when a word was clearly mislabeled (132 words, 3.8% of the list; mostly adjectives mislabeled as nouns). When a word can act as more than one part of speech depending on context, I left the tag as-is and deferred to NLTK as the established framework, using the primary, most common label. Here I also used an LLM strictly to help flag potential errors in NLTK’s output.

Both lists rank words by frequency, then apply learner-focused curation. Michael West’s 1953 list especially reflects period pedagogy. He favored general-purpose vocabulary over emotional or highly specific words, not just whatever appeared most often (Therova, 2020, summarizing West, 1953, pp. ix–x). Some of what looks like “1950s life” may also be how mid-century ESL teaching filtered the language. I still treat the lists as a portrait of everyday English because both cover a large share of running text and speech that goes well beyond the classroom.

title: Copyright Scammers Weaponized Meta's Rights Manager with Backdating Exploit
description: Scammers are allegedly exploiting a flaw in Facebook's 'Edit Post' feature to backdate stolen videos and hijack copyright claims.
fullText:
Similar to other social media platforms, creators on Facebook and Instagram have to battle a constant stream of copyright infringing material.

To facilitate this process, the company has rolled out several anti-piracy initiatives in recent years.

Both Facebook and Instagram use a “Rights Manager” tool, which is an automated system that runs copyright checks. After rightsholders upload reference files, the system detects infringing material and allows owners to take down or monetize this content.

Rights Manager has been working without much noise for close to a decade. According to Meta’s latest transparency report, Rights Manager is part of a broader enforcement system that proactively removes millions of infringing posts from Facebook and Instagram every month.

The automated copyright enforcement system is not without flaws. In India, for example, several lawsuits filed at the Delhi High Court alleged that the same copyright enforcement system can be turned against the creators it is meant to protect.

The Rights Manager exploit relies on Facebook’s desktop “Edit Post” feature. When a user edits an existing Facebook post and replaces its attached image or video, the platform keeps the original publication date. This means that users and Meta’s enforcement systems will see the content as older than it really is.

Scammers can allegedly exploit this weakness, Bar and Bench first reported. They can edit their older Facebook pages to add videos, reels, or photos they copied from other creators. To Instagram and Facebook it will appear that their content is older, so they can use it to claim ownership through Rights Manager.

As a result, the scammers can reportedly monetize videos of the original creators, while adding strikes to their accounts too.

Financial educator and entrepreneur Pushkar Raj Thakur says at least 36 of his videos were taken down worldwide this way. His suit argues Meta acted on the claims without checking the rightsholder, metadata or edit history of the posts.

Thakur took the matter to the Delhi High Court in May as part of a broader lawsuit about false claims. Early on, Meta’s counsel said the company needed to investigate, but the false claims did not stop right away.

In a follow-up hearing, Meta offered the court a series of assurances. It agreed not to remove Thakur’s videos over copyright strikes, not to close his account over repeat strikes, and to restore the deleted content.

Thakur is not backing down, seeking roughly 2 crore rupees (about $210,000) in damages. He also wants the court to order Meta to build safeguards into Rights Manager, including KYC checks, timestamp protections, and metadata verification.

Interestingly, Thakur says Meta denied him access to Rights Manager to protect his own brand, even as the scammers used the very same tool against him.

Thakur’s lawsuit is not the only one. Another creator, Neeraj Joshi, filed a similar complaint over the same backdating trick, and this case already resulted in a more actionable order.

On July 9, Justice Jyoti Singh required Meta to preserve Joshi’s verified Instagram account and to hand over the basic subscriber information and IP logs tied to the fraudulent claims within three weeks.

Those records could reveal who is behind the scheme and Joshi’s request for an interim injunction will be heard on August 5.

The two lawsuits are not the only pressure on Meta. On July 15, another creator, Nitin Joshi, filed a public interest litigation (PIL) that goes after the legal framework itself.

The petition asks the court to set up a Special Investigation Team to probe what Joshi describes as an organized extortion racket, where syndicates file bogus strikes through bot accounts and then demand payment to withdraw them.

It also challenges Rules 3(1)(c) and 4 of India’s IT Rules, arguing they let platforms disable accounts without notice, without naming the complainant, and without checking whether the claimant owns the content.

Joshi wants a forensic audit of Instagram’s copyright strike system, as well as regular transparency reports on repeat complainants. This case remains in its early stages, and it has yet to be heard.

For now, the three cases leave Meta with an unusual problem. The same automated system that’s used to remove millions of infringing posts is allegedly being used by scammers to monetize copyright infringement.

Monthly proactive Instagram removals

Whether Meta has already addressed the loophole, and whether the scammers will be unmasked, remains to be seen. The company has yet to respond to the allegations in court, and it hasn’t commented publicly on the claims.

In any case, it appears that Meta has some work to do on the transparency side as well. At the time of writing, its most recent copyright transparency report is more than two years old, covering 2023.

A copy of the order in the Neeraj Joshi case is available here (pdf). The July 1 order in the Pushkar Raj Thakur case can be found here (pdf), and the earlier May 29 order is here (pdf).

title: Meta disregarded its own research on teen harm, Tennessee tells jury
description: Attorneys for the state of Tennessee told a jury in Nashville on Monday that Meta Platforms' leadership disregarded internal research about its Instagram
fullText:
July 27 (Reuters) - Attorneys for the state of Tennessee told a jury in Nashville on Monday that Meta Platforms' leadership disregarded internal research about its Instagram platform's impact on teenagers as the company sought to maximize profit from young ‌users.

During opening statements in a seven-week trial in state court in Tennessee, the state's lawyers said Meta researchers repeatedly flagged that ‌some teenagers were compulsively using the platform, leading to eating disorders, depression and self-harm. But despite those warnings, Meta did not disable features such as autoplay, notifications and infinite scroll ​that, the lawyers said, were designed to keep teens on Instagram as long as possible and increase the number of ads they viewed.

An attorney for Meta countered that the company has been transparent about the risks teens face on Instagram and the amount of dangerous content that it finds. The company works hard to find problems and fix them, he said.

The lawsuit, filed by Tennessee Attorney General Jonathan Skrmetti's office, seeks financial penalties and a ‌court order directing Instagram to modify aspects of ⁠the platform that the state says are harmful to teens' mental health.

If the jury finds the company liable, the trial will enter a second phase before Chancellor Russell Perkins, the judge overseeing the trial, who will decide whether ⁠to order the company to pay financial penalties and make changes to Instagram to make it safer for teens.

During the opening statements, which Reuters watched on Courtroom View Network, Tom Cartmell, a lawyer for the state, played the familiar dinging sound of a notification hitting a smartphone. Unpredictable rewards like notifications trigger dopamine hits ​that ​promote addiction, which has a particularly strong impact on the brains of kids, Cartmell ​said.

Meta understood the brain science behind why teens find ‌its platform so irresistible, Cartmell said.

Cartmell showed the jury an internal document from 2017 in which Meta product managers wrote that features like notifications and infinite scroll "are inherently at odds with well-being" and said that the company needed to warn the public.

"This warning never came," Cartmell said.

BROADER LEGAL BATTLE OVER PLATFORMS

Kevin Huff, a lawyer for Meta, said documents like those Cartmell cited are proof that the company is searching for problems on its platforms, so it can improve them.

The company has developed tools to help limit problematic use of Instagram, and seeks to empower teachers and parents to help ‌keep teens safe, Huff said.

Huff urged jurors to consider whether Meta should bear sole ​responsibility for societal problems such as suicide, child exploitation and addiction. "We think the evidence ​will show that Meta is doing its part and empowering others ​to do their part, because protecting teens online is a shared responsibility. It takes a village."

Nearly every state in ‌the country has filed claims against Meta over its platforms' ​alleged impact on children. More than ​two dozen of the lawsuits have been consolidated in multidistrict litigation in San Francisco, while many other states have sued in their own courts. Separately, Meta and other social media companies are facing thousands of lawsuits brought by individuals and school districts.

Tennessee's lawsuit is the ​second state case to reach a jury. Earlier ‌this year, a jury in New Mexico found the company liable and ordered it to pay $375 million. A judge is weighing ​additional financial penalties as well as an order directing the company to change Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp in the state.

title: See county maps of states linked to cyclosporiasis outbreak
description: Data collected by USA TODAY shows where reported cyclosporiasis cases are concentrated and which communities have been hardest hit.
fullText:
A cyclosporiasis outbreak has spread to nine states, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said July 24, as the intestinal illness that causes weeks of severe and "explosive" diarrhea continues to sicken thousands of Americans, with case counts still climbing.

The nine states linked to the outbreak are Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania and West Virginia.

Cases have been reported in 41 states, the CDC said. However, the federal data lags state data for weeks. The agency is still investigating the illnesses unrelated to the multistate outbreak.

The CDC noted on July 24: "This outbreak may not be limited to the states with known illnesses, and the true number of sick people is likely much higher than the number reported. This is because many people recover without medical care and are not tested for Cyclospora."

USA TODAY has collected figures directly from several state health departments to show where reported cyclosporiasis cases are concentrated and which communities have been hardest hit.

Latest updated map tracking 'explosive diarrhea' cases in the US

Michigan leads the nation in cyclosporiasis cases, with more than 9,200 cases as of July 27, and 160 hospitalizations reported as of July 23. Wayne County has the most cases, with over 1,000, followed by Washtenaw and Oakland counties, according to county-level data from the state Department of Health and Human Services.

When the population is taken into account, Shiawassee County is the hardest-hit county with about 592 cases per 100,000 residents. That's nearly double the rate reported in Lenawee County, the next-highest at about 335 cases per 100,000 residents.

Cyclosporiasis updates: CDC says these four states are likely linked in outbreak

Ohio is another state that reported a record number of cyclosporiasis cases, with over 2,500 cases confirmed, based on the latest data available through July 23.

Lucas County reported the state's highest number of cases with 435, followed by Wood County with 309 and Sandusky County with 186. Sandusky County has the state's highest infection rate at about 317 cases per 100,000 residents, followed by Fulton County and Wood County.

More: The best electrolyte drinks for diarrhea as cyclosporiasis cases rise

As of July 22, the state received 468 reports of cases of cyclosporiasis, and 177 cases have been confirmed.

"While cases of cyclosporiasis normally rise in the spring and summer months, Kentucky is one of many states experiencing a larger-than-typical increase," said Beth Fisher, spokesperson at Kentucky Cabinet for Health and Family Services.

Fisher said Kentucky typically only has about 35 cases of cyclosporiasis each year.

Jefferson County, home to Louisville, has the state's most cases, at 37, and Washington County has the state's highest case rate at about 32 cases per 100,000 residents.

In West Virginia, cases are concentrated in the state's northern panhandle. The state reported 226 cases as of July 24, with Hancock County leading at a rate of 83 cases per 100,000 residents.

Indiana has reported more than 800 cases as of July 27. Allen County saw the most cases, 144, followed by Marion County and Elkhart County. Steuben County has the state's highest infection rate at about 129 cases per 100,000 residents, followed by DeKalb County and Harrison County.

As of July 22, Kansas reported 289 cases in total. Johnson County had the state's most cases, at 95, but Osage County had the state's highest infection rate at 45 cases per 100,000 residents.

Illinois reported 513 cases with 39 hospitalizations as of July 23. Matthew Mata, the state's health public information officer, said the county-level data is not available at the moment.

Oklahoma had 172 cases as of July 20, and county-level data is not available.

The state's health department confirmed 45 cases in 2026 so far. The county-level data is not available.

As of July 24, Connecticut confirmed 62 cyclosporiasis cases since May. Western Connecticut Planning Region had the most cases, with 33. That's about five cases per 100,000 residents.

Florida reported 158 cases since May, based on the state's Department of Health's latest report as of July 18. With 33 cases, Miami-Dade County leads in the state, followed by Lee County and Broward County.

Arizona has reported 19 cases this year. According to Magda Rodríguez, spokesperson with the Arizona Department of Health Services, none of those cases are associated with localized clusters or active outbreaks in Arizona.

Nevada has reported two cases of cyclosporiasis since May 1, both in Clark County. Daniel Vezmar, a spokesperson for the Nevada Department of Health and Human Services, said the state has no evidence that the cases are linked to the nationwide outbreak.

This story was updated to reflect the latest available data for each state.
